text: Can vibration cut stone? In a factory, today, yes. Can sound cut or lift the stones of a pyramid? That is a different claim. This episode keeps the two apart: what engineers have published, what experiments with ancient tools found, what people claim, and what would settle it.

First, the real method. It is called ultrasonic machining. A metal tool vibrates along its length, somewhere between eighteen and forty thousand times a second, too fast to hear, by about a tenth of a millimetre or less. Between the tool and the work flows a slurry: water full of hard grit, such as silicon carbide or boron carbide. Each vibration drives grit grains into the surface. In a hard, brittle material, each hit chips off a speck. Millions of specks later, there is a hole in the shape of the tool.

Notice who does the cutting. Not the tool. The grit. The tool is usually ordinary steel, softer than the glass or ceramic it cuts. Vibration is only a way to keep slamming fresh grit into the surface, again and again.

None of this is anyone's personal discovery. A 1927 paper by Robert Wood and Alfred Loomis is credited with first discussing ultrasonic machining. Lewis Balamuth filed a British patent in 1945, and an American patent is listed as issued in 1952. Machines were being built in the nineteen fifties. A 1998 review by Thoe, Aspinwall and Wise, in the International Journal of Machine Tools and Manufacture, surveys decades of work. Sources disagree on which machine was the first.

It has limits. It works best on hard, brittle materials: glass, ceramics, gemstones, stone. Springy metals mostly absorb the hits. It is slow. It makes holes and cavities, usually in small parts, and deep holes are hard, because fresh slurry struggles to reach the bottom. And it needs a power supply and a transducer, piezoelectric or magnetostrictive, to turn electricity into vibration. It is not a way to quarry large blocks.

Now the ancient side. Egyptian granite sarcophagi carry saw marks, recorded by Flinders Petrie in the eighteen eighties and by others since. Granite is hard, and the craftsmen had copper tools. How? In 1999 the experimental archaeologist Denys Stocks tested it at the Aswan quarries, and reported in Antiquity in 2001. His copper blade was one point eight metres long, with quartz sand under it, and two people pulling it back and forth.

It cut. Slowly: about twelve cubic centimetres of granite an hour, dry or wet, and he suggested that experience could double that. The sand did the cutting; the soft copper just carried it, and the copper wore away too. This is a published experiment. It shows what can work. It does not prove what the Egyptians did.

Look at the family resemblance. Egyptian sand sawing and ultrasonic machining both drive hard grit into hard stone with a softer tool. The difference is the motion. By hand, it is a stroke or two a second, our own estimate. Ultrasonic machining is twenty thousand or more. That is roughly ten thousand times as many hits, in tiny strokes, with electronics to make them. A cousin, not the same thing.

Now the claim. Some authors argue the Egyptians used ultrasonic drilling. The best known version is the engineer Christopher Dunn, in a 1984 magazine article. He compared a spiral cut that Petrie measured in a granite core with the feed rate of a modern diamond drill, and concluded the ancient rate was about five hundred times greater. Egyptologists dispute that, and experiments show copper tubes with sand can cut granite. We found no ancient transducer, no power source, and no text describing one. Claimed. Not established.

The other claim is bigger: that sound lifted the blocks. Stories describe drums and trumpets floating stones. Episode two met the same idea at Coral Castle. We found no film, measurement or physical trace we could check. What does real acoustic levitation do? In labs, sound waves hold small, light things in the air. The heaviest object held by far field levitation is listed as a six tenths of a gram foam ball. A close range method can carry several kilograms, but only hundreds of micrometres above a vibrating surface.

Here is our own rough arithmetic. An average Great Pyramid block is about two and a third tonnes, an estimate. Hold one up with sound under one flat square metre. Even with perfect reflection, you would need roughly one hundred eighty six decibels. Air itself tops out near one hundred ninety four, where the pressure swing equals the whole atmosphere. And the block weighs almost four million times that foam ball. That does not prove it impossible. It shows the size of the gap.

What would settle it? For cutting: independent labs comparing tool marks on ancient stone with marks made by known methods, ultrasonic included. For lifting: a recorded demonstration with a stone of known weight, measured sound levels, and a second team repeating it. Any find of a device would count. And one bench test anyone can do: an ultrasonic cleaner, a copper strip, grit and soft stone, the same minutes with vibration on and off, then measure the groove. We have written that plan. We have not run it, so we have no result.

So here is the ledger. Documented: ultrasonic machining cuts hard, brittle materials. Egyptian granite has saw marks. Copper and sand cut granite, slowly, in Stocks's tests. Disputed: how the drill holes were made. Claimed: that ancient builders used ultrasonic tools. Not established: that sound cut or lifted pyramid stones. Unknown here: whether vibration speeds up copper and sand cutting, because our test has not been run.

So, can vibration cut stone? Yes, with grit, a transducer, and electricity. Did anyone do it in the pyramid age? Not established. Did sound lift pyramid blocks? Not established, and the arithmetic is steep. Not ruled out, either. That is for evidence to settle. If you can run a test, someone watching this might be the one who shows us.
